Vostok 1. Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961. The mission lasted 108 minutes and completed one complete orbit of Earth. Gagarin monitored systems during the flight, but Vostok 1 was fully automated, controlled from the ground.

The spacecraft had a re-entry capsule that Gagarin sat atop, exposing him to extreme heat and G-forces during descent. Yet he survived, becoming an instant international hero. But there was a secret the Soviet Union kept for years: Gagarin ejected from the capsule and parachuted back to Earth separately. This fact would have violated the rules of competition for the Space Race, which required the cosmonaut to land in the spacecraft, so the Soviets said nothing.

The Soviet Union had designed and launched Vostok, giving them a decisive early victory in the Space Race. Their success intensified international competition for space achievement. Vostok missions continued with subsequent flights, including Vostok 6, which launched in 1963, carrying Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space. Through these early missions, the Soviets demonstrated technological prowess and pushed the boundaries of what humans dared attempt in the vacuum above.
